                    REPLY BRIEF AND PROTEST OF ENCHANTED ROCK

        Pursuant to Rule 2111 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or

“Commission”)’s rules of practice and procedure, and ordering paragraphs (D) and (E) of the

Order on Show Cause Proceeding, Directing Compliance Filings, Establishing Paper Hearing,

and Granting in Part and Denying in Part Complaint, issued by the Commission on December

18, 2025,2 Enchanted Rock, LLC (“Enchanted Rock”) hereby files this reply brief and protest

(collectively, “Protest”) to: 1) respond to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) initial brief,

submitted on February 23, 2026;3 and 2) respond to PJM’s February 23, 2026 compliance filing

submitted in response to the Commission’s December 18 Order.4

          This Protest challenges a limitation that PJM seeks to impose related to the provision of

Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (“Interim NITS” 5). More specifically, as

described by PJM to stakeholders – but not set forth in its Initial Brief, Illustrative Tariff or the

February 23 Compliance Filing – PJM intends to prohibit Co-Located Load from receiving any

capacity or energy from a Co-Located Generating Facility while the Co-Located Load is taking

Interim NITS (sometimes referred to herein as the “Proposed Interim NITS Limitation”).6 For

the reasons set forth below in further detail, PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation runs afoul

of the Commission’s applicable findings and directives in the December 18 Order, including

Commissioner Rosner’s unequivocal statements in his concurring opinion to the December 18

Order explaining that a Co-Located Load “can take service directly from the generator” while the

Co-Located Load is taking Interim NITS7 (sometimes referred to herein as the “Interim Period”).

         Moreover, PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation, if enacted, would make it

commercially impractical for Eligible Customers to ever utilize Interim NITS to serve their Co-

Located Load, thus undermining the Commission’s goals of establishing Interim NITS in order

to “facilitate the timely provision of transmission service to Eligible Customers taking

 transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Loads, while preserving reliability for other

transmission customers,”8 and to address interconnection delays faced by large load

interconnection customers.9

        For these reasons, and the reasons set forth herein, Enchanted Rock respectfully requests

that in any final order issued in the above-captioned proceedings, that the Commission 1) hold

that PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation is prohibited, and 2) direct PJM to file revisions to

its tariff to clarify that a Co-Located Load can be served by its Co-Located Generating Facility

during the Interim Period, consistent with the applicable holdings and directives in the December

18 Order.

I.       BACKGROUND

        i.       Justification for Interim NITS

        In response to the Commission’s February 20, 2025 order to show cause,10 several parties

recommended that “the Commission explore the potential to develop a new level of non-firm or

interruptible transmission service that prioritizes connection of new flexible loads, regardless of

whether they are co-located with generation.”11 Among these parties was Enchanted Rock,

which filed extensive comments supporting the establishment of a new, interim non-firm

transmission service to enable large load customers to interconnect faster while maintaining

overall reliability of the transmission system.12

        As the Commission recognized in its December 18 Order, “Enchanted Rock supports a

transitional non-firm service where the load relies on PJM to provide energy, but where the load

 is under a commitment to dispatch co-located generation during PJM curtailments.”13 The

Commission further recognized that Enchanted Rock proposed that “the co-located facilities

could be quickly interconnected and would only require curtailment in a small number of hours

of a year, allowing more efficient use of generation resources and transmission capacity,

lowering costs to customers, and buying time for new infrastructure to be built.”14

        The Commission noted that in order to “facilitate more rapid interconnection and

operation of Co-Located Loads” PJM and other parties discussed “the development of a new

transitional service that would allow new Co-Located Load to withdraw electricity from the PJM

transmission system earlier than may be otherwise achievable if those new Co-Located Loads

could only be designated as Network Load and served once all of the Network Upgrades

necessary to provide the requested NITS are complete.”15

        ii.      Commission Directives Related to Interim NITS

        In response to these parties’ comments, the Commission directed PJM to “create a new

interim, non-firm transmission service . . . [to] allow an Eligible Customer that has requested

NITS on behalf of a Co-Located Load to take non-firm transmission service that can be

interrupted until the Network Upgrades necessary to provide NITS are complete and the Co-

Located Load can be designated as Network Load.”16 This “new interim, non-firm transmission

service” is what PJM defines as “Interim NITS.”

        The Commission further held that Interim NITS would help to address interconnection

delays faced by large load customers by “allowing an Eligible Customer that has requested to

take NITS on behalf of a Co-Located Load to, through this new transmission service, receive an

 interruptible transmission service before the Network Upgrades necessary to designate and serve

the Co-Located Load as Network Load are complete.”17 Moreover, the Commission held that

“when curtailed, Eligible Customers taking this transmission service on behalf of Co-Located

Loads may be able to continue to take energy from the Interconnection Customer with which

they are co-located if PJM’s Tariff otherwise allows.”18 The Commission directed PJM to file

tariff revisions implementing this new service.19

        Notably, in his concurring opinion to the December 18 Order, Commission Rosner

described the Commission’s rationale behind ordering the establishment of Interim NITS in

further detail, as well as how it is intended to be implemented in practice:

        today’s order directs PJM to establish a new interim service (see Figure 4) to
        provide a bridge while the infrastructure needed to serve a large load with
        traditional front-of-meter network transmission service is being built. This interim
        service leverages speed in the near-term and unlocks the benefits of a full grid
        connection in the long-term. It will allow co-located loads and generators seeking
        front-of-meter service to access the grid faster than they can today. In exchange for
        increased speed, these loads will bear the risk of being curtailed when the grid is
        constrained until the transmission upgrades needed to provide service are
        constructed. But that doesn’t mean that the load will always have to shut down
        completely during peak periods. Rather, if the co-located load is paired with a
        new generator, and that generator is still waiting to begin its own front-of-meter
        service, the load can take service directly from the generator in the interim until
        both “graduate” to full, front-of-meter service. This pathway is important because
        traditional, front-of-meter network transmission service provides the broadest
        benefits to both load and generators—a network load can be served by any
        generator on the grid, and a network generator can sell its power to any customer
        on the grid.20

        Additionally, in Commissioner Rosner’s Figure 4 describing Interim NITS, it states that

the “Generator can serve load while awaiting grid connection or when grid is unavailable.”21

 Accordingly, as made unequivocally clear by Commissioner Rosner’s concurring statements, the

Commission intended for a Co-Located Load taking Interim NITS to be able to utilize energy

and capacity provided by a Co-Located Generating Facility during the period in which the Co-

Located Load and Co-Located Generating Facility are being studied for full NITS (i.e., during

the temporary Interim Period). This makes sense, as large load customers (particularly data

centers), cannot bear commercial risks associated with being fully offline for any material

amount of time, meaning that in order to utilize Interim NITS, Co-Located Load will need to be

served by their Co-Located Generating Facilities during periods in which they may be curtailed.

         iii.     PJM’s Proposed Implementation of Interim NITS

         In response to the Commission’s directives related to Interim NITS in the December 18

Order, PJM filed the February 23 Compliance Filing (which provided a “shell” of Tariff, Part XI,

to show that Interim NITS will be housed in a new Part XI of PJM’s Tariff22), and its Initial

Brief, including the Illustrative Tariff.23 Sections 700-707 of Subpart A, Part IX of PJM’s

Illustrative Tariff contain the non-rate terms and conditions related to PJM’s proposed

implementation of Interim NITS.

         Notably, nowhere in PJM’s February 23 Compliance Filing, Initial Brief or applicable

sections of its Illustrative Tariff does PJM make any mention of Proposed Interim NITS

Limitation. Notwithstanding this fact, PJM has clearly indicated to its stakeholders that when it

actually implements Interim NITS, it intends to ensure that “Co-located load taking Interim

NITS service will not have rights to the capacity/energy from any specific co-located

II.      PROTEST

         i.       The Proposed Interim NITS Limitation Cannot Be Imposed by PJM Because it is
                  Not Part of PJM’s Filed Rate

         While none of PJM’s February 23 Compliance Filing, its Initial Brief or Illustrative Tariff

make any mention of Proposed Interim NITS Limitation,26 PJM instead seeks to impose the

Proposed Interim NITS Limitation through means not specified in the PJM Tariff. However, any

prohibition on a Co-Located Load’s ability to be served by a Co-Located Generating Facility

during the Interim Period must be specified in the PJM Tariff, as the prohibition significantly

impacts how Eligible Customers taking Interim NITS must operate their Co-Located Load

during periods in which they are curtailed, and as discussed further below in Section II.ii, renders

Interim NITS entirely unworkable. Therefore, because the Proposed Interim NITS Limitation is

certainly a practice “that affect[s] rates and service significantly, that [is]

reasonably susceptible of specification, and that [is] not so generally understood in any

contractual arrangement as to render recitation superfluous,” it must be included within the PJM

Tariff (i.e., PJM’s filed rate) in order to be effectuated.27 PJM has not included any language

 intended to implement the Proposed Interim NITS Limitation in its Illustrative Tariff, meaning

that it cannot be imposed by PJM.

        ii.      PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation Would Render Interim NITS
                 Unworkable and Conflicts With the Commission’s Directives in the
                 December 18 Order

        As noted previously, the Commission established Interim NITS in order to allow “an

Eligible Customer that has requested to take NITS on behalf of a Co-Located Load to . . .receive

an interruptible transmission service before the Network Upgrades necessary to designate and

serve the Co-Located Load as Network Load are complete.”28 The core purpose of Interim NITS

is to allow a large load customer to interconnect faster in exchange for being interruptible (i.e.,

curtailable) when the transmission system is stressed and firm transmission service must be

prioritized for Network Customers taking NITS. Importantly, Interim NITS is designed to be

temporary,29 and only be in place until Network Upgrades are constructed, and both the Co-

Located Load and Co-Located Generating Facility can take or provide full Network Service,

respectively. This is reflected clearly in Commissioner Rosner’s concurrence to the December 18

Order, in which he stated that “if the co-located load is paired with a new generator, and that

generator is still waiting to begin its own front-of-meter service, the load can take service

directly from the generator in the interim until both ‘graduate’ to full, front-of-meter service.”30

        PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation would prohibit Co-Located Generating

Facilities from serving Co-Located Load during the Interim Period, which would mean that the

Co-Located Load would be exposed to actual shutdowns when curtailed. Absent the ability to be

 served by the Co-Located Generating Facility, the Co-Located Load would in fact “always have

to shut down completely during peak periods,”31 – which is the precise outcome that the

Commission sought to avoid by seeking to instead enable the “[co-located] load [] [to] take

service directly from the generator in the [I]nterim [Period].”32

        Based on Enchanted Rock’s experience, large load customers, which Interim NITS is

designed to serve, will accept the risk of being curtailed in exchange for faster interconnection.

However, these customers cannot commercially bear the risk of being completely shut down

when curtailed. Data centers and similar critical infrastructure facilities typically operate under

contractual reliability requirements demanding continuous uptime of 99.999% or greater.

Market rules that would require these customers’ Co-Located Loads to be curtailed, but that

would allow a Co-Located Generating Facility to serve the Co-Located Load while it is being

curtailed, would be operationally and commercially manageable. However, PJM’s Proposed

Interim NITS Limitation forecloses that option and would effectively force large load customers

taking Interim NITS to risk actually being shut down during periods in which they are curtailed,

rendering Interim NITS commercially impractical and unworkable.

        Other parties agree with Enchanted Rock’s assessment of PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS

Limitation. As noted by the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”) in their answer to PJM’s February

23 Compliance Filing, the DCC stated that the Proposed Interim NITS Limitation “is unworkable

because curtailment should limit use of the grid, not prevent the customer from using the co-

located resource it supplied, which supports Interim NITS in the first place. If the customer

cannot use that generation during curtailment, Interim NITS provides no practical value.”33

 Similarly, Crusoe Technologies LLC noted that “[i]f large load customers cannot rely upon their

own Co-Located Generating Facilities . . . during the Interim NITS period, it would create a

significant disincentive and effectively nullify Interim NITS as a viable transmission service

option and commercial pathway.”34

        For the foregoing reasons, the Proposed Interim NITS Limitation plainly conflicts with

the Commission’s holdings and directives related to Interim NITS in the December 18 Order and

undermines the entire Interim NITS market construct. For these additional reasons, the Proposed

Interim NITS Limitation is not just and reasonable and must not be permitted to stand by the

Commission.35

 III.    CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, Enchanted Rock respectfully requests that the Commission

consider this Protest. Moreover, Enchanted Rock respectfully requests that in any final order

issued in the above-captioned proceedings, that the Commission 1) hold that PJM’s Proposed

Interim NITS Limitation is prohibited, and 2) direct PJM to file revisions to its tariff to clarify

that a Co-Located Load can be served by its Co-Located Generating Facility during the Interim

Period, consistent with the applicable holdings and directives in the December 18 Order.
